extracted.intended_audience: systematic reviewers, biomedical researchers, journal editors, policy-makers and health professionals involved in evidence-based decision making
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, classifying, measuring and reducing dissemination (publication and related) biases in biomedical research and in the conduct and appraisal of systematic reviews; includes definitions, study inclusion/search/classification methods, cohort types, and recommended assessment/scoring approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissemination bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when the dissemination profile of a study’s results depends on the direction or strength of its findings. The dissemination profile is defined as the accessibility of research results or the possibility of research findings being identified by potential users. The spectrum of the dissemination profile ranges from completely inaccessible to easily accessible, according to whether, when, where and how research is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term to embrace publication and related biases; emphasizes accessibility (when, where, in what format) and that publication is a continuum rather than a dichotomy. Consider dissemination profile (accessibility) rather than a simplistic published/unpublished label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when the publication of research results depends on the nature and direction of the results. Because of publication bias, the results of published studies may be systematically different from those of unpublished studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize publication bias as one component of dissemination bias; can lead to misleading literature syntheses if published studies are a biased sample of all conducted studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when a study in which multiple outcomes were measured reports only those that were significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider selective outcome reporting as a form of incomplete publication; systematic reviewers should be alert to discrepancies between protocols/registrations and reported outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time lag bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when the speed of publication depends on the direction and strength of the trial results. For example, studies with significant results may be published earlier than those with non-significant results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine time-to-publication in cohorts; time lag can distort apparent effects in the literature at any given time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grey literature bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when the results reported in journal articles are systematically different from those presented in reports, working papers, dissertations or conference abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic reviewers should search for grey literature (reports, dissertations, conference abstracts) to reduce bias; inclusion/exclusion of grey literature affects dissemination profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when the full publication of studies that have been initially presented at conferences or in other informal formats is dependent on the direction and/or strength of their findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track subsequent full publication of abstracts/conference presentations; consider abstract-to-full publication rates and their association with results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when languages of publication depend on the direction and strength of the study results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that restricting reviews to particular languages (e.g. English) can introduce bias if positive results are more likely published in certain languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple publication bias (duplicate publication bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when studies with significant or supportive results are more likely to generate multiple publications than studies with non-significant or unsupportive results. Duplicate publication can be classified as ‘overt’ or ‘covert’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detecting covert duplicate publication is difficult; reviewers should check for overlapping data and report potential multiplicity to avoid over-counting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when the place of publication is associated with the direction or strength of the study findings. For example, studies with positive results may be more likely to be published in widely circulated journals than studies with negative results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider journal prominence/circulation as a potential source of bias when assembling evidence; place influences dissemination and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when the chance of a study being cited by others is associated with its result. For example, authors of published articles may tend to cite studies that support their position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that searching by citation and scanning reference lists may yield a biased sample; reference-scanning can propagate citation bias into reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Database bias (indexing bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when there is biased indexing of published studies in literature databases. A literature database, such as MEDLINE or EMBASE, may not include and index all published studies on a topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on a single database; use multiple bibliographic databases and consider that index coverage may be associated with study results (indexing bias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media attention bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when studies with striking results are more likely to be covered by the media (newspapers, radio and television news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media coverage can affect dissemination independent of formal publication; consider media influence when assessing accessibility and prominence of findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissemination profile (continuum of accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The accessibility of research results or the possibility of research findings being identified by potential users; ranges from completely inaccessible to easily accessible, according to whether, when, where and how research is presented or stored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dissemination profile to assess and categorise accessibility rather than binary published/unpublished status; informs choice of methods to detect/reduce bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of measures to deal with dissemination bias (pre/during/post review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Available methods for dealing with dissemination biases were classified according to measures taken before, during or after a literature review: to prevent publication bias before a literature review (e.g. prospective registration of trials), to reduce or detect publication and related biases during a literature review (e.g. locating grey literature or unpublished studies, and funnel plot related methods), and to minimise the impact of publication bias after a literature review (e.g. confirmatory large-scale trials, updating systematic reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate interventions at each stage: encourage prospective registration and reporting guidelines pre-review; comprehensive searches and statistical methods during review; confirmatory studies and updates post-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal solution: prospective, universal registration of studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal solution to publication bias is the prospective, universal registration of all studies at their inception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote trial/study registries covering clinical trials, observational and early-stage research; registries only reduce publication bias if results become accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of statistical methods as sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Available statistical methods for detecting and adjusting publication bias should be mainly used for the purpose of sensitivity analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat statistical detection/adjustment methods (e.g. funnel plots, trim-and-fill) as indirect/exploratory tools with assumptions; use them to assess robustness rather than to definitively correct bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for inclusion of evidence and method studies in review
rubrics_metrics.description: Included studies were those that provide empirical evidence on the existence, consequences, causes and/or risk factors of types of dissemination bias; and method studies were those that develop or evaluate methods for preventing, reducing or detecting dissemination bias in biomedical or health-related research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting a methodological review, classify studies as evidence (empirical) or method studies; some studies may be both. Focus on direct evidence but include indirect when direct is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature search strategy and iterative searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Search a range of health-related/biomedical bibliographic databases (e.g. MEDLINE, Cochrane Methodology Register, EMBASE, AMED, CINAHL, PubMed, PsycINFO, OpenSIGLE) for an appropriate time period; because methodological literature is poorly indexed, adopt an iterative approach by examining references, citations and focused searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple databases and timeframes; supplement formal searches with reference checking and citation tracking to reduce missed methodological studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of identified studies and evidence types
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify identified studies according to framework of dissemination profile into non-publication (never or delayed), incomplete publication (outcome reporting or abstract bias), limited accessibility (grey literature, language or database bias), and other biased dissemination (citation, duplicate or media attention bias). Also separate empirical evidence studies into direct and indirect evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map studies to bias types; prioritise direct evidence (admissions, comparisons between published/unpublished, prospective cohorts) and use indirect evidence where direct is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohort study types (inception, regulatory, abstract, manuscript)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohort studies of publication bias were classified according to the starting point of follow-up: inception cohort (follow-up from study beginning), regulatory cohort (studies submitted to regulatory authorities), abstract cohort (abstracts presented at conferences and subsequent full publication), and manuscript cohort (manuscripts submitted to journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose cohort framing appropriate to the research question; different cohort types have different implications for what can be inferred about publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of publication and classification of study results
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication was usually defined as full publication in journals, but publication is a continuum; study results were commonly classified as ‘statistically significant (p ≤ 0.05)’ versus ‘non-significant (p > 0.05)’ or ‘positive’ versus ‘non-positive’ with examples of labels for positive (favourable, significant, striking) and non-positive (negative, inconclusive, null).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about operational definitions used for ‘published’ and for result categories; acknowledge subjectivity in labels like positive/negative and consider sensitivity analyses using different classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and categorisation of systematic reviews for assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a representative sample, search MEDLINE for 'systematic review' or 'meta-analysis' and categorise identified reviews into treatment effect, diagnostic accuracy, epidemiological (risk factors), and gene-disease association reviews; then select random samples from each category for assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate review types because dissemination bias may differ across them; use random sampling and clearly report sample sizes and selection strategy to enhance representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data extraction and reviewer procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Initially extract data independently by two reviewers using pre-defined data extraction forms; resolve disagreements by consensus. If standard forms are insufficient, extract data directly into study tables with checking by a second reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dual extraction for reliability; be flexible if rigid forms are inadequate but maintain independent checking. Document extraction methods and resolution processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment caveat (difficulty applying checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Planned to apply a checklist of quality assessment to appraise empirical studies but found it extremely difficult because of poor reliability of the checklist and heterogeneity of study designs; therefore did not apply the checklist but summarised main limitations narratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limitations of applying a single quality checklist across diverse methodological and empirical studies; where checklists are unreliable, provide transparent narrative assessment of limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring system for efforts to minimise publication bias and risk levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures taken to deal with publication and related biases in a systematic review were judged as ‘sufficient’, ‘partial sufficient’ or ‘insufficient’. Risk of publication bias was considered to be ‘low’, ‘moderate’ or ‘high’ accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a pre-derived scoring system to rate efforts and risk; apply the tool consistently and report judgments and criteria used for each level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis heterogeneity assessment and software
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, results were quantitatively pooled; heterogeneity across studies was measured using the I2 statistic. Meta-analyses were carried out using Review Manager (RevMan Version 5.0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess heterogeneity (I2) before pooling; use established meta-analysis software and report methods and heterogeneity measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended priorities for future research on dissemination bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Further empirical research is needed to evaluate the effect of prospective registration of studies, open access policy and improved publication guidelines; investigate the role of developments in computer science and information technology for prevention of dissemination bias; study the impact of publication bias on health decision-making and patient management outcomes; develop qualitative methods to assess risk of publication bias in systematic reviews; focus on practical application of available statistical methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design empirical and methodological studies to address these priorities; focus on applicability to reviewers and decision-makers and on translating registry/access initiatives into accessible results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures to minimise impact of research dissemination bias in systematic reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: In systematic reviews, measures can be taken to minimise the impact of research dissemination bias by systematically searching for published and unpublished studies. Trial registers will only be helpful in reducing publication bias if the results of registered trials are accessible. All statistical methods, simple or complex, are by nature indirect and exploratory, and are often based on certain assumptions that can be difficult to justify. The available statistical methods can be useful for the purpose of sensitivity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement comprehensive searches including unpublished sources and trial registries with accessible results; use statistical methods cautiously as sensitivity analyses and transparently report assumptions and limitations.
